title: Against harm
hookLine: a prayer against those who seek to harm; teachers stress praying against evil, not people
last: KINDNESS AND JUSTICE, FROM THE SAME THRONE.

cards: A group of thugs lives in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood. The Talmud doesn't say exactly what they did, only that they caused him a great deal of trouble.
And Rabbi Meir, one of the great teachers of the Mishnah, does what plenty of us would do. He prays that they die. His wife, Beruriah, hears him.
She's a scholar in her own right, one of the few women the Talmud quotes on points of law. And she asks him a question about a verse.

teach.b: The twelfth blessing of the weekday Amidah is a prayer against those who do harm.
The Talmud, in Berakhot 28b, says it was added later than the others: Rabban Gamliel asked who could compose it, and Shmuel the Small stood up and did.
That's how the eighteen blessings became nineteen. Its wording has changed many times over the centuries, and scholars still debate exactly whom it first meant.

Today it asks that slanderers have no hope and that wickedness vanish, and it ends: blessed are You, who breaks enemies and humbles the arrogant. It's a prayer born of real danger. So how should it be said?
Back to Beruriah, in Berakhot 10a. She points to Psalm 104. In the old Jewish translation: "Let sinners cease out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more."

But the Hebrew letters for sinners, she says, can also be read as sins. Let sins cease. Then look at the second half: if the sins are gone, the wicked will be no more, because they'll no longer be wicked.
Pray that they turn around. Rabbi Meir does, and the Talmud says they did. That story has shaped how many teachers read this blessing ever since.
Even with real enemies, the target is the harm, not the person who might still change.

how: The twelfth blessing of the weekday Amidah, against slanderers and wickedness, appears in different wordings in different prayer books; many teachers explain it through Beruriah's reading that the prayer is for sins to end, not sinners.

o: a prayer that harm ends, not the people who do it
a prayer for the safety of travelers on the road

games.q: you're Rabbi Meir. neighborhood thugs are making your life miserable. your wife Beruriah quotes Psalm 104. what does she suggest?
games.why: let sins cease: if the sins end, the wicked will be no more. he prayed for them to repent, and the Talmud says they did.

practice: Name one harm in your world, a bully at school, a cruel post going around, someone who keeps hurting someone you love, a wrong in the news, and let yourself feel the anger honestly.
Then try Beruriah's move: separate the harm from the person, and hold the wish that the harm stop and, if you can manage it, that the person doing it turn around. If you pray, you can ask for that.

wordCard.voice: Against harm. The Amidah's twelfth blessing, the one added at Yavneh, read through Beruriah: let sins cease, not sinners.

orig.note: Hebrew in Psalm 104:35: sinners. Beruriah noted that the letters can also be read as sins.

carryVoice: Your line: end the harm. The wish is not for people to vanish, but for the harm to end. See you tomorrow.
